items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1976-02-04
items.q: INTERVIEWER: Do you, do you think that, that Jelly Roll Morton had the wide popularity among blacks that Louis Armstrong did when he was alive? [INTERVIEWEE] Never, never, never, never. Jelly, Jelly played in, clubs, and he made records that were popular...

ctx.x: there was some, a feeling, I guess, you know, he was glad to, he was sorry to leave Louie, because he and Louie was the famous duets they did, you dig?
Do you, do you think that, that Jelly Roll Morton had the wide popularity among blacks that Louis Armstrong did when he was alive?

Never, never, never, never. Jelly, Jelly played in, clubs, and he made records that were popular, but to actually have, he moved around too fast. See, if he just stayed like, in Chicago, and worked in clubs, they stationary, like you make a reputation in the town, like Fletcher Henderson was in New York, Cab Calloway were in New York at the Cotton Club, Fletcher at the Roseland, you heard him on the radio, Duke was at the Cotton Club, you heard him on the radio, Earl Hines in, in the Grand Terrace in Chicago for…

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I’m around, he say, “You think you can get me six cockroaches?”, after I knew him a while. Said, “Yeah, I think I can get you six cockroaches.” ... We played the gig.

ctx.x: Just had paid for it. A four-string banjo. The kind Kimball had. Kimball was a star around here. I wanted the same kind, and I could play it pretty good. Get to New York with a banjo. I’m around there for about two weeks. While I’m there they take me to the Rhythm Club, Paul and Red Allen. Rhythm Club was where . . . They had about three clubs around there: the Mimo Club, the Rhythm Club, and the Band Box. Three clubs where the musicians hung out at. There, every day I get introduced to different musicians. Paul…

size, but he’s older than me, much older than me. Paul said, “Look out for my nephew, Steele.” Steele said, “All right. I’ll look out for him. Is he all right? Is he wise, or he’s a fool?” Paul say, “He’s not a fool. He’s partly wise, Southern wise.” They kidding and joking. Every day I’d see Steele around, and Steele is showing me all these people. The second day out of there . . . The first day they brought me there, went in the Rhythm Club, there was King Oliver and Jelly Roll [Morton] playing pool. Fletcher…

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewer mentions Jelly Roll Morton in the context of Black Benny, but the interviewee (Danny Barker) does not mention Jelly Roll Morton in his response, nor does he describe any personal interaction or relationship with him.

ctx.x: No, they never . . . They had military funerals for whites. If he was a general in the army, or he was a navy man, or he belonged to one these artillery . . . They had a whole lot of artillery, batallion societies that they kept going all the time. Different branches of service. The brigade. They did something. They honored . . . they was fighting the battle of Jericho and the walls came tumbling . . . All that . . . So they have a nice sweet military funeral. The navy or the marine band or the army band would…

You mentioned a lot of legendary people in the brass band: Manny Perez. Black Benny, who Louis Armstrong talks about. Jelly Roll [Morton] talks about him. Who were some of the people you saw that had eventually come to have big names, because I imagine you saw a lot of these people before they left New Orleans for good, before the late teens.

Red Allen. Guy Kelly. I didn’t see Jimmie Noone, because he left around 1917, 1918, ’19, ’20, and I wasn’t old enough to realize what I was looking at, knew who these people were. But I knew of them, that they went away. I heard of the Baquet family. I heard of Sidney Bechet. He was a legend. He went when he was around 16 years old. He started traveling with carnival shows and minstrel shows. He was such a phenomenon at that time. People had never heard nobody blow a horn like that. He was a frustrated trumpet…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: Jelly Roll would stand out in front of the club and talk to all these defeated musicians; half of them couldn't play, including me. We'd stand around there waiting for a gig and looking up at Jelly Roll.

ctx.x: He was kind of tall, and he smiled all the time. But he had a strange name. He would be in there. And James P. Johnson would come through there. Fats Waller come through there.

Jelly Roll stood on the corner. They didn't understand Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll would be talkin' like he talked to night people, who understand Jelly Roll... Jelly Roll would stand out in front of the club and talk to all these defeated musicians; half of them couldn't play, including me. We'd stand around there waiting for a gig and looking up at Jelly Roll. Well, Jelly Roll is from home. But Jelly Roll, he loves an audience. I noticed Jelly Roll had two little things on the end of his jaw that he could establish…
